title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair versus two pointers guided by the sorted order.

content.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted

blocks.text: Given a 1 indexed array of integers numbers that is already sorted in non decreasing order, find two numbers that add up to a specific target, and return their 1 indexed positions.

blocks.caption: Two pointers from both ends, moving based directly on comparing the sum to the target

blocks.text: Given a 1 indexed array of integers numbers that is already sorted in non decreasing order, find two numbers that add up to a specific target, and return their 1 indexed positions.

blocks.title: Analogy: Balancing a Scale With Sorted Weights
blocks.text: Like having a row of weights already arranged from lightest to heaviest, and needing to pick exactly two that balance a target value, using the sorted arrangement to know instantly which direction to search next.

blocks.caption: Find the pair of numbers in the sorted array that adds up to the target

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["2 plus 7 equals 9","a valid pair at positions 1 and 2","These are the two values whose sum exactly matches the target"],["Answer","[1, 2]","The 1-indexed positions of the two numbers that sum to 9"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["2 plus 4 equals 6","a valid pair at positions 1 and 3","2 and 4 are the two values, not necessarily adjacent, that sum to the target"],["Answer","[1, 3]","The 1-indexed positions of 2 and 4"]]}

blocks.text: Negative numbers work exactly the same way: -1 plus 0 equals -1, giving [1, 2].

Before checking pairs blindly, notice the array being sorted is not incidental information, it is the single fact that determines exactly which direction to search next at every step, without ever having to guess.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If the sum of the current smallest and largest candidates is too small, the only way to make it larger is to replace the smaller of the two with something bigger; since the array is sorted, that means moving the left pointer rightward, never the right pointer.

Observation 2: Symmetrically, if the sum is too large, the only way to make it smaller is to replace the larger candidate with something smaller, which means moving the right pointer leftward.

Observation 3: This means at every single comparison, exactly one direction is ever correct to move in, no guessing, no need to try both, since the sorted order rules out every other possibility with certainty.

Observation 4: Because the two pointers only ever move toward each other, never apart, and never revisit a position, the entire array is scanned at most once in total, giving a linear pass instead of a quadratic all-pairs check.

Whenever both a target-sum question and a sorted input appear together, the sorted order is the signal to reach for two pointers converging from both ends, since it guarantees exactly one correct direction to move at every step.
This is the canonical two-pointer template that every other "sorted array, find a pair or triple with some sum property" problem builds on, from 3Sum to Container With Most Water.
Check every pair of positions directly, adding their values and comparing against the target.

items: For every index i, check every later index j.
If numbers[i] plus numbers[j] equals target, return their 1 indexed positions.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The inner loop starts at j = i + 1, never at j = 0, so the same pair is never checked twice and an index is never paired with itself.
The function returns 1-indexed positions directly at the point of the match, since the problem explicitly asks for 1-indexed positions, not the more common 0-indexed ones.
The function returns as soon as a match is found, since the problem guarantees exactly one valid pair exists, so no further searching is ever needed once it is located.

blocks.text: Every pair is directly checked, so the one valid pair is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), checking every pair.
Space: O(1) extra, no additional structure is used.

Limitation: this completely ignores the fact that the array is already sorted, which allows the search direction to be determined instantly at every step instead of checking every combination blindly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Checking every pair treats the array as if it carried no useful structure at all, re-deriving from scratch, for every single pair, information that sortedness already answers directly: whether the current pair's sum needs to grow or shrink to reach the target. Once that direction is known, there is exactly one sensible move, adjust whichever end is responsible, and trying anything else would be provably wasted effort, since sortedness guarantees no pair skipped this way could have been the answer. Starting from the two extremes and letting the comparison decide the next move, every step, collapses an all-pairs search into a single directed walk that never revisits ground already ruled out.

Use two pointers, one starting at the very first position and one at the very last. If the sum of the two values is too small, the only way to increase it is to move the left pointer inward to a larger value, since the array is sorted. If the sum is too large, move the right pointer inward to a smaller value. Repeat until the target sum is found.
Two pointers from both ends, guided directly by comparing the current sum to the target.

blocks.caption: Optimized: two pointers from both ends, moving based directly on comparing the sum to the target

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), the pointers together traverse the array at most once.
Space: O(1) extra.

At every step, the current sum being too small or too large rules out an entire set of possibilities in one comparison: if the sum is too small, every pair using the current right value paired with anything smaller than the current left value would be even smaller still, so only increasing the left pointer can ever help; symmetrically for a too-large sum. Because each move permanently eliminates a range of pairs that could never have been the answer, and the two pointers only ever converge, never diverge or repeat, every possible valid pair is guaranteed to be checked, or correctly ruled out, by the time the pointers meet.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Comparison result","Correct move"],"rows":[["Current sum equals target","Return the current positions immediately"],["Current sum is less than target","Move the left pointer rightward, toward larger values"],["Current sum is greater than target","Move the right pointer leftward, toward smaller values"]]}

items: left and right start at the two true ends of the array, before any comparison has been made.
current_sum is recomputed fresh at every iteration, since either pointer may have moved since the last comparison, changing what value it now represents.
The three-way branch, equal, too small, too large, exhaustively covers every possible outcome of comparing current_sum to target, leaving no case unhandled.
The returned positions add 1 to each 0-based index, directly converting to the 1-indexed positions the problem requires.

blocks.text: This is the canonical two pointer problem: sortedness turns "which direction should I search" into a direct, guaranteed correct decision at every single step, removing the need to check every combination.

items: Applying the hash map approach from the unsorted Two Sum problem here, which works but ignores the O(1) space, O(n) time two pointer solution that the sorted input specifically enables.
Returning 0 indexed positions instead of the 1 indexed positions the problem explicitly asks for, an easy off-by-one mistake when adapting the standard unsorted Two Sum's return convention.

Moving the wrong pointer when the sum is too large or too small, for instance moving the right pointer inward when the sum is too small, which would never bring the sum closer to the target and could loop without ever finding the answer.

items: Explicitly contrast this with the unsorted Two Sum problem, explaining that sortedness is precisely what allows trading the O(n) space hash map for an O(1) space two pointer scan.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find a pair summing to a target, and the array is already sorted" points toward two pointers from both ends immediately, since sortedness is the signal that a hash map's extra space is no longer necessary.

items: How would you find all pairs summing to the target, not just one? Continue moving both pointers inward after recording a match, skipping past any duplicate values to avoid repeated pairs, instead of returning immediately.

How would this extend to Three Sum, finding a triple summing to a target? Fix one value with an outer loop, then run this exact two-pointer scan on the remaining sorted sub-array for the other two values.

What if numbers were not sorted? Either sort it first, paying O(n log n) upfront to then use this O(n) two-pointer scan, or fall back to the O(n) time, O(n) space hash map approach used for the original unsorted Two Sum.
The canonical template for every "sorted array, converging two pointers" problem, extended directly in Three Sum, 3Sum Closest, and 4Sum.
Same "move whichever side is responsible for the sum being off-target" logic as Container With Most Water, just with a different quantity, sum vs. area, being compared against a target.
Same foundational two-pointer convergence structure as Reverse String, though driven here by a sum comparison instead of an unconditional swap.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Two pointers converging from both ends of a sorted array, guided by comparing the current sum to the target
Core Idea: Sortedness guarantees exactly one correct direction to move at every step: increase the left pointer when the sum is too small, decrease the right pointer when it is too large
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)

Most Important Observation: A sorted input paired with a target-sum question is the classic signal to trade a hash map for a two-pointer scan, since sorted order alone determines the correct move at every step
Interview Difficulty: Easy to Medium
One-line memory trick: Too small, move left up; too big, move right down
